item.title: Create a Memoir Depicting Current Times
item.description:
Memory

Create a Memoir Depicting Current Times

Reflecting on today’s events and crafting memories to treasure can be uplifting.

Posted June 30, 2026

Key points
  • Either gratitude or recollection of trauma may be triggered by today’s atmosphere.
  • Documentation is a valuable help to our personal history.
  • Know when it’s time to hit the reset button.
  • Consider the value of writing a gratitude memoir.
Stop for a moment to view a honey bee.
Source: REWatson, 2026

We often think of memoir writing as the depiction and recreation of past experiences. However, this particular time in our lives is rich with opportunities to capture thoughts and feelings in a present day memoir. Unlike a personal journal, memoir reflections are to be shared with others.

Just think of the array of emotions encountered in these few months: From graduations and family celebrations to World Cup games and patriotic parades. Political divisions seemed to dissipate on soccer fields and basketball counts. And despite the rivalry, players on both teams displayed admirable moments of respect for one another.

A memoir might be a reflection of this current time and how events affect you. To these, incorporate an earlier memory or memories, and a memoir begins to take shape.

Either gratitude or recollection of trauma may be triggered by today’s atmosphere

In taking part in celebrations, today’s happenings might trigger feelings of gratitude. And if so you may merge the thoughts with other times in your life when gratitude seemed to ground you.

Conversely you might recall trauma in your life that may begin to dissipate as a result of writing about the experience.

Dr. James W. Pennebaker, Professor Emeritus at the University of Texas, Austin, in a podcast interview for the American Psychological Association explained that “memoir helps us to view our life story with objectivity.”

In exploring trauma, he determined that “having a trauma of any kind and keeping it secret really increased the toxicity of that trauma, secrets in and of themselves were toxic.”

Speaking with Kim Mills, he added:

“And this made me wonder: If secrets are so bad, what if we brought people in the laboratory and had them talk about them or—that turned out to be way too complex. How about we just had them write about it? And that was kind of the birth of expressive writing.” (Mar 2024).

Documentation is a valuable help to our personal history

Documentation helps with tracing facts as well as emotions, the highs and lows in life that affect us. Such documentation is especially valuable when reviewing chaotic or difficult times. How challenging times impact us and those we love is important personal history.

Know when it’s time to hit the reset button

During stressful times it is easy to fall into a lethargic pattern in which days blend together and spirits lag. However, there is still time, at the year’s half point, to hit the reset button.

Using the written word, begin photographing feelings so that each day you can begin to capture a memorable moment. Unlike biography, think of the memoir as creative non-fiction. Purdue University’s OWL notes:

“The Creative Nonfiction (CNF) genre can be rather elusive. It is focused on story, meaning it has a narrative plot with an inciting moment, rising action, climax and denouement, just like fiction. However, nonfiction only works if the story is based in truth, an accurate retelling of the author’s life experiences.”

Instead of laboring over exact dates, places, and time, capture the essence of your story. Write about the feelings that the memory elicits.

  • Did a smile come to your face?

  • Did you tingle with excitement?
  • Or do you still shudder when recalling the trauma?

Consider the value of the gratitude memoir

Writing a gratitude memoir during difficult and often angry times might seem to be a bit of an oxymoron. Nonetheless, instead of falling into the “misery loves company” trap, create a vision. Bring yourself to a place that inspires you whether it’s traveling abroad or visiting places within your own neighborhood.

Take a walk through a garden or park. Sit on a bench or in the grass. Listen to the birds. Watch bunnies hopping along.

When you need to feel grounded, think of the world of Sue Stuart-Smith, a British psychiatrist. With her husband, an avid gardener, she wrote, The Well-Gardened Mind.

“All gardens exist on two levels – the real garden on the one hand and the imagined or remembered one on the other. . .”

In talking about her own garden she wrote, “This grove has a life of its own in my imagination, and I can turn to it at any time of year.” (p. 68)

When walking through a garden, walk slowly so that you can marvel at a butterfly flitting from one flower to the next. Listen to the breeze as it fans the leaves. Stand still when you see a bee so you can watch the bee hugging a flower. Let every experience become part of the tapestry you are weaving, the tapestry called a memoir.
